directive: Valerius expands the personal guard to fifty infantry and fifty cavalry, with ten infantry and ten cavalry drawn from the twenty newly added local veterans and the remaining forty infantry and forty cavalry drawn from his established veterans, each retaining singular tactics and individual equipment while fighting in perfect unison.

events.title: VALERIUS ORDERS THE PERSONAL GUARD DOUBLED
events.body: At the opening of July, Valerius orders the personal guard expanded from the twenty men formally established in the previous round to a permanent body of one hundred. The order is precise: fifty are to serve as infantry and fifty as cavalry, with ten infantry and ten cavalry drawn from the twenty newly admitted local veterans and the remaining eighty places filled by veterans from Valerius's own established men. The expansion does not create new manpower from outside the expedition; it reorganizes selected veterans already serving under Valerius into a defined personal-guard establishment. Every selected veteran is entered by name, branch, primary weapon, and individual fighting method rather than being treated as an interchangeable file. Valerius makes clear that the guard's purpose is not to erase individual skill but to place many distinct skills inside one disciplined command structure.

events.title: TEN OF THE NEW VETERANS TAKE THE INFANTRY LINE
events.body: Titus Varenus, Lucius Atilius, Gnaeus Fabius, Marcus Lartius, Publius Servilius, Quintus Vibius, Sextus Tullius, Aulus Decimus, Numerius Cassius, and Spurius Calpurnius are designated among the guard's fifty infantry. Their earlier weapons remain part of their identities, but their roles are now fitted into a larger infantry body whose movement follows the established outward-facing perimeter and open interior doctrine. Each veteran retains the method by which he distinguished himself during the proving and induction, while learning to give way, close gaps, and hold position in relation to the other guard members. Their local knowledge is treated as an additional reason for keeping their positions flexible rather than rigidly identical. The ten therefore become the first nucleus of the new guard infantry without ceasing to be the men Valerius personally inducted.

events.title: THE OTHER TEN NEW VETERANS ARE MOUNTED
events.body: Gaius Valerius, Lucius Marcius, Marcus Petronius, Publius Octavius, Quintus Rufrius, Titus Manlius, Gnaeus Licinius, Sextus Cornelius, Aulus Furius, and Lucius Vettienus are assigned to the cavalry half of the new guard. Their individual weapons remain distinctive, but each man receives the necessary mounted equipment and adapts his established method to the movement of a horse without being reduced to a generic cavalry role. Valerius specifically preserves their differences: the spear men retain reach, the javelin users retain their screening function, and the swordsmen retain their close-escort roles. The ten veterans practice mounting, dismounting, changing position, and returning to the guard's wider formation without breaking its cohesion. By evening, the newly added veterans have been divided evenly between the two branches while remaining one personal guard under one command.

events.title: FORTY OF VALERIUS'S ESTABLISHED VETERANS ENTER THE INFANTRY GUARD
events.body: Forty veterans from Valerius's own established men are selected to complete the infantry half of the hundred-man guard. Their names and individual equipment are entered into the new register, with each man retaining a singular method rather than being assigned an anonymous standardized role. Some favor swords, others spears, javelins, slings, shields, or combinations of these, and the differences are deliberately preserved as part of the guard's character. What changes is their relationship to one another: the veterans drill their individual methods around common spacing, signals, and movement so that one man's specialty does not interrupt another's position. The established veterans therefore become a second, larger foundation beneath the ten newly added local veterans in the infantry branch.

events.title: FORTY ESTABLISHED VETERANS COMPLETE THE CAVALRY GUARD
events.body: A further forty of Valerius's established veterans are selected for the cavalry branch, bringing the mounted guard to its full strength of fifty. Each receives or retains equipment suited to his own method, and the roster records the distinction between a man's weapon and the collective duty he performs. The mounted veterans practice remaining mutually supportive while moving through different positions around Valerius rather than behaving as forty separate riders. Their horses, weapons, and individual habits are brought under the same discipline that already governs the expedition's foot soldiers. By the end of the day, Valerius has a cavalry guard whose diversity is visible in every line of the register but whose command relationship is singular.

events.title: ONE HUNDRED DISTINCT FIGHTERS MOVE AS ONE
events.body: An unscheduled field movement gives the enlarged guard its first opportunity to function as a hundred-man body rather than as separate infantry and cavalry appointments. The infantry closes and opens its spacing as the cavalry passes around it, while individual veterans continue to use their own preferred weapons and methods without breaking the movement of the men beside them. The result is striking precisely because no one has surrendered his individuality: the guard's differences become complementary instead of competitive. The twenty local veterans in particular are able to pass information and adjust their positions without waiting for a separate command structure, while Valerius's established veterans provide the larger body of experienced coordination around them. No battle occurs, but the exercise demonstrates that the expanded guard can preserve its singular fighters while moving according to one coherent discipline.

events.title: THE HUNDRED-MAN PERSONAL GUARD IS ESTABLISHED
events.body: By the close of the round, Valerius's personal guard stands at one hundred men: fifty infantry and fifty cavalry. Twenty of those places belong to the veterans newly admitted in the previous rounds, divided evenly between foot and horse, while eighty are filled by veterans drawn from Valerius's established body of men. Every member has an individual weapon and a distinct fighting method recorded beside his name, yet the guard is trained to move, protect, and respond as one formation. The arrangement does not increase the expedition's total soldier count because every guard member was already part of Valerius's existing manpower; it changes their assigned status and organization. The result is a formally defined personal guard whose strength lies not in uniformity of equipment but in the disciplined combination of many specialized veterans.
